summary: Jesus withdraws from the Pharisees’ plot to the Sea of Galilee, where crowds from every region press on Him, and Matthew sees Isaiah’s gentle Servant fulfilled.
key_insight: Matthew does not attach Isaiah’s words to the miracles. He attaches them to Jesus’ withdrawal and His order to keep quiet. The Servant who “will not quarrel nor cry out” fulfilled Scripture by stepping away from a fight and from fame.
story: The Pharisees had gone out to plot against Jesus. When He knew it, He withdrew from there {Mt} with His disciples to the sea. {Mk}

A great multitude from Galilee followed Him, and from Judea and Jerusalem and Idumea and beyond the Jordan. A great multitude from around Tyre and Sidon came to Him as well, when they heard how many things He was doing. {Mk}

Jesus told His disciples to keep a small boat ready for Him because of the crowd, lest they should crush Him. He had healed many, and everyone who had an affliction pressed toward Him to touch Him. {Mk} He healed them all. {Mt}

Whenever the unclean spirits saw Him, they fell down before Him and cried out, “You are the Son of God.” But He sternly warned them that they should not make Him known. {Mk} He warned the people, too, not to make Him known. {Mt}

So the word spoken by Isaiah the prophet was fulfilled: “Behold! My Servant whom I have chosen, My Beloved in whom My soul is well pleased!” God would put His Spirit upon Him, and He would declare justice to the Gentiles. {Mt}

“He will not quarrel nor cry out, Nor will anyone hear His voice in the streets. A bruised reed He will not break, And smoking flax He will not quench,” until He brings justice to victory, “And in His name Gentiles will trust.” {Mt}
differences: Only Mark lists the regions the crowds came from, including Idumea, Tyre and Sidon, and mentions the boat kept ready and the crowd pressing to touch Him.
Matthew says Jesus warned the people He healed not to make Him known; Mark says He sternly warned the unclean spirits.
Matthew says He healed “them all”; Mark says “He healed many,” as the reason the crowd pressed in.
Only Mark records the spirits’ cry, “You are the Son of God.” Only Matthew quotes Isaiah 42:1–4.

fit.question: Matthew’s quotation does not match Isaiah 42 as it reads in the Old Testament. Isaiah has “My Elect One in whom My soul delights” and “the coastlands shall wait for His law”; Matthew has “My Beloved in whom My soul is well pleased” and “in His name Gentiles will trust.” Did Matthew misquote Isaiah?

points.label: Translating as he quoted
points.text: Matthew wrote in Greek and quoted a Hebrew prophet. Like other New Testament writers, he sometimes translated straight from the Hebrew, sometimes used the Greek translation of his day (the Septuagint), and sometimes rendered freely for the sense. His last line follows the Septuagint, which says the Gentiles will hope in His name.

points.label: Wording that points to the baptism
points.text: “My Beloved in whom My soul is well pleased” is a fair rendering of Isaiah’s “My Elect One in whom My soul delights,” and it sounds like the Father’s voice at the Jordan: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Matthew lets the reader hear that Isaiah’s Servant and the Father’s beloved Son are one.

points.label: The same hope
points.text: In Isaiah, the coastlands are the distant lands of the nations. Coastlands waiting for His law and Gentiles trusting in His name describe the same hope in different words.

fit.note: Matthew quotes Isaiah faithfully in meaning, translating and explaining as he goes, as the apostles commonly did. The differences show care, not carelessness.
fit.short: Matthew translates Isaiah for the sense, partly following the Greek Septuagint, and words it to echo the Father’s voice at Jesus’ baptism.

scene.label: Idumea
scene.text: Idumea was the old land of Edom, south of Judea. Its people had been forced to accept circumcision and Jewish law in the late second century BC, and Herod the Great’s family came from there. This is the only time the New Testament names it. With Tyre and Sidon on the coast to the northwest, Mark’s list reaches nearly every border of the land.

scene.label: Pressing to touch
scene.text: Many believed that touching Jesus, even His clothes, would heal them (Mark 5:28; 6:56). With a great crowd pushing forward at once, someone could be trampled. A small boat standing just offshore gave Jesus room to step back from the press.

scene.label: The Servant of the Lord
scene.text: Isaiah 42:1–4 is the first of several passages about the Lord’s chosen Servant (Isaiah 42; 49; 50; 52:13–53:12). The Servant brings justice to the nations, and in the last of them He suffers and dies for His people. Matthew has already applied Isaiah 53:4 to Jesus’ healings (Matthew 8:17).

scene.label: Bruised reed, smoking flax
scene.text: Reeds grew thick along the Jordan and the lake; a bruised one was cracked and nearly worthless. A lamp’s wick was made of flax, and when the oil ran low it smoldered and smoked. Most people would snap the one and pinch out the other.

witnesses.matthew: Sets the scene right after the plot to destroy Jesus and gives it his longest Old Testament quotation. In Matthew, Jesus’ withdrawal and His call for silence are not weakness; they fulfill Isaiah’s picture of a Servant who does not quarrel. The quotation names the Gentiles twice, looking ahead to the end of his Gospel: “make disciples of all the nations” (28:19).
witnesses.mark: Gives the crowd’s map, from Idumea in the south to Tyre and Sidon on the coast, and the practical detail of a boat kept ready so the crowd would not crush Him. Unclean spirits fall before Him and name Him rightly, and He silences them. In Mark, knowing who Jesus is is not the same as following Him.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is God’s chosen Servant, full of the Spirit and strong enough to bring justice to victory, yet gentle with the bruised and the barely burning. He would not fight for His reputation or let demons announce Him.
seeing.living: The people pressing around Jesus that day were bruised reeds: sick, tormented, some from pagan Tyre and Sidon. They nearly crushed Him, and He did not crush them. If your faith is barely smoking, bring it to Him as it is; He does not snuff out what is weak.
seeing.ponder: Where are you a bruised reed or a smoking wick, and do you believe Jesus will be gentle with you there?

preaching.big_idea: God’s chosen Servant wins His victory without quarreling and without crushing the weak.
outline: The Servant steps away from the fight (15–16)
The Servant who will not crush (19–20)
preaching.watch_for: The word “Gentiles” comes twice in the quotation (18, 21). Just after Israel’s leaders plot against Jesus (12:14), Matthew points to the nations who will trust in His name.

title: Crowds by the Sea: God’s Chosen Servant
